summary: How to make remote MANUAL control of the bit-exact iPhone browser feel smooth — comprehensive root-cause + architectural options, weighed against the fingerprint moat.

contributors.cause: Per-touchMove WebDriver /actions POST serialization on the box (touch input path, NOT video)
contributors.evidence: This is the founder's 'not just latency' contributor and the single most damaging one for SCROLL specifically. Path (verified): GUI fires send({type:'touchMove'}) on EVERY raw DOM mousemove with NO rAF/throttle coalescing (apps/gui-client/src/lib/livekit-input-capture.ts ~line 467) → each becomes its own DataChannel publishData(reliable:false) → DataChannelInputReceiver serially dispatches each (single FIFO consumer, LiveKitVideoPublisher inboundConsumerTask awaits each to completion) → injectTouchStreamMove → ONE synchronous HTTP POST /session/:id/actions per move (WebDriverClient.swift:700-704) with body pointerMove duration:16 (touchStreamMoveActions, line 681-685). W3C Actions ticks BLOCK the WebDriver server for the move duration, so each touchMove costs ~16ms+ of serialized server time PLUS the POST/HTTP round-trip on the box. A mouse drag emits 60-125 mousemove/s but the box can only drain ~30-60 POSTs/s (16ms floor each, serial) → the input queue BACKS UP, so the finger position the fork sees LAGS the real cursor by a growing backlog, and scrollBy is driven by stale, bursty, unevenly-spaced deltas → choppy/erratic scroll that worsens the faster you drag. This is independent of video fps and of RTT. Fix class: rAF-coalesce touchMove emit to ~1/frame on the GUI, and/or batch buffered moves into a single multi-tick /actions POST on the box, and/or drop duration to 0/1ms for live moves.

contributors.cause: Open-loop feedback: scroll has NO local prediction, so every drag waits a full round-trip to become visible
contributors.evidence: The GUI renders only the incoming video; touchMove does not move anything locally. So the perceived scroll latency = GUI emit + ~150-180ms NL->US customer leg (one way) + box input-drain/inject + fork scrollBy repaint + SCStream capture + encode + ~150-180ms US->NL return + jitter buffer = ~300-400ms round-trip before the user sees their own drag move (12fps already = 83ms/frame quantization on top). Founder's key datapoint (docs/internal/streaming-latency-region-fix.md, CORRECTION 2026-06-21): NL->US RDP over the SAME trans-Atlantic path is smooth/'1000x faster', which PROVES raw RTT is not the bottleneck — RDP hides RTT with local cursor echo + its own frame clock. Our pipeline has neither, so the same RTT reads as lag. Magnitude is real (~300ms loop) but it is a multiplier on the other defects, not the root; an EU box cuts it to ~10-30ms but the doc explicitly says that is NOT the fix.

contributors.cause: Software VP8 encode is the default codec (libwebrtc auto-negotiation), not hardware H.264
contributors.evidence: v1.0 default path is LiveKitVideoPublisher → libwebrtc encoder, and the default codec is VP8 (harness-streaming-bridge.md line 22: 'libwebrtc encodes (VP8)'). videoPreferredCodec defaults to nil = auto = VP8 software (libvpx) unless DRIFTSTACK_VIDEO_CODEC=h264 is set (LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift:229-234). Software VP8 is CPU-bound and competes with the WebKit fork render on the same box (~20 sessions/host target), and the SDK stats explicitly flag this case: qLimit=cpu + encoder=libvpx => ENCODER-bound (line 1067). Hardware VideoToolbox H.264 on Apple Silicon offloads to the media engine = lower encode latency + frees CPU for render. This both raises encode latency per frame and starves the fork repaint (compounding the supply-fps cause). Fix is a known env flip (DRIFTSTACK_VIDEO_CODEC=h264), already plumbed and being pinned by A3.

contributors.cause: Supply-limited fork repaint cadence: SCStream only delivers .complete (changed) frames, so a static/occluded page yields ~2-5 real fps
contributors.evidence: CaptureLoop drops idle/blank frames, keeping only .complete (CaptureLoop.swift shouldProcessFrame, line 512 + delegate filter line 764) — SCStream is change-driven, so the fork only emits a new frame when its WebContent actually repaints. An occluded/idle/paint-once fork window delivers ~2-5fps (streaming-latency-region-fix.md line 46; pump comment lines 74-80 cite '~2-5fps... the founder 1000x slower than RDP'). The 12fps measured is consistent with a SUPPLY-bound stream (qLimit=none, framesEncoded≈framesSent≈fps, line 1068), i.e. the fork isn't repainting at 30Hz during/after a scroll. The frame pump (startFramePump, line 769) re-feeds the LAST buffer at videoMaxFps to keep the wire smooth, but it duplicates a STALE frame — it does NOT produce new scroll content, so during an actual scroll the user still only gets new pixels at the fork's real repaint rate. Real fix is the fork-side layer-volatility / IOSurface keepalive so the off-screen WKWebView repaints at 30-60Hz (referenced CaptureLoop.swift:354-359, A1/fork lane).

contributors.cause: WebRTC jitter buffer / playout delay adds buffering latency and, when minimized, re-exposes choppiness
contributors.evidence: The GUI subscribe side is already maxed for low latency (adaptiveStream:false, dynacast, setPlayoutDelay(0)) per the founder brief and streaming-latency-region-fix.md line 18-19 ('A2 maxed the subscribe side... Neither moved the needle'). With playout(0) the receiver de-jitters minimally, which is correct for latency but means any uneven inter-frame arrival (from the bursty supply fps + variable encode + trans-Atlantic jitter) is shown as judder rather than smoothed. So the jitter buffer is not ADDING much latency anymore, but it also can no longer mask the upstream irregularity — it is a minor residual, dependent on fixing the supply/codec/input causes first. Note maxBitrate/buffer tuning operates only on the ~33-66ms capture+encode budget (region-fix line 31).

contributors.cause: GUI input mapping: mouse->touch with no emit-rate control + fling replayed as more touchMoves over the same congested path
contributors.evidence: The mouse->touch translation itself is coherence-correct (genuine pointerType:touch, tapSlop/deadzone, EMA velocity, computeFlingPath inertial glide — livekit-input-capture.ts). But the inertial fling REPLAYS the decelerating glide as a stream of timed touchMove events (line 351, 377) down the SAME per-POST-serialized path, so a flick injects an extra burst of moves that queue behind the live drag and arrive late. And the lack of any emit-side rAF/throttle (covered as the dominant cause) is a GUI-input design gap. Minor on its own — it amplifies the box-side serialization rather than being an independent stall — but the fling-as-touchMoves and unthrottled emit both live in the GUI layer and should be coalesced there.

contributors.cause: GUI video rendering / per-frame copies and capture pipeline overhead
contributors.evidence: GUI rendering is a standard attached LiveKit <video> element and is not implicated by any diagnostic; not a measured contributor. On the box side there are TWO full-frame ~1.4MB memcpys per frame (CaptureLoop Data copy + LiveKitVideoPublisher.makePixelBuffer per-row copy; zero-copy-capture-design.md), adding small per-frame latency + CPU that competes with render at fleet density — but the doc itself rates this low-urgency ('stream already smooth') and a latency/scaling win, not the cause of the choppiness. DRIFTSTACK_VIDEO_ZEROCOPY is designed but default-off. Minor.

contributors.cause: Box-side per-touchMove WebDriver HTTP round-trip + W3C pointerMove duration:16ms, strictly serialized through ONE FIFO inbound consumer
contributors.evidence: The most-overlooked contributor, NOT latency-or-fps. In .incremental mode (default, ManualTouchInjector.swift:57) every touchMove is its OWN blocking WebDriver /actions POST: DataChannelInputReceiver.dispatch -> inj.touchStreamMove -> WebDriverClient.injectTouchStreamMove (WebDriverClient.swift:700) -> postJSON to the fork localhost WD server. The body is touchStreamMoveActions with duration max(1,durationMs) defaulting to 16ms (WebDriverClient.swift:681-684); a W3C pointerMove with non-zero duration ANIMATES synchronously server-side before the POST returns. These POSTs run on a SINGLE serial consumer: LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift:380 'for await data in stream { await self.dispatchInboundData(data) }', and dispatchInboundData awaits ir.receive() to completion before reading the next message. So touchMoves cannot pipeline: each costs ~16ms + localhost HTTP overhead (~1-5ms), and they queue head-of-line. A fast click-drag emits ~60-120 mousemoves/s (one touchMove each) but the box drains at only ~40-60/s, so input BACKS UP: the drag lags the finger and keeps scrolling after release as the backlog drains. A transient WD stall freezes ALL subsequent input. Distinct from and compounding the ~12fps problem.

contributors.cause: ~12fps SUPPLY-limited video: the fork WebContent repaint cadence delivered verbatim via change-driven SCStream, compounded by software VP8 encode
contributors.evidence: A3's root-cause (bus W2745/W2746), agreed by both agents: ~12fps is the fork's real repaint cadence delivered verbatim. SCStream is change-driven: CaptureLoop.makeStreamConfiguration sets minimumFrameInterval as a CEILING not a floor (CaptureLoop.swift:453) and only .complete (new-content) frames pass shouldProcessFrame (CaptureLoop.swift:512; idle/blank dropped). The frame-pump (LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift:73-92) re-feeds the last buffer at 30fps when idle but correctly yields to real frames DURING a scroll, so delivered fps during motion = the fork's ~12. At 12fps frames are ~83ms apart, so even with zero network a scroll updates in ~83ms steps = choppy. Compounded by codec: VideoQualityCollector logs qLimit/encoder (LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift:1070) to disambiguate qLimit=cpu+encoder=libvpx (software VP8, CPU-bound) from qLimit=none (supply/repaint-bound); A3 pinned DRIFTSTACK_VIDEO_CODEC=h264 to HW VideoToolbox to free CPU. Dominant because at 12fps everything looks choppy regardless of input; founder's headline feels-awful (bus W2747). Magnitude: 12fps -> ~83ms inter-frame vs 30fps -> 33ms.

contributors.cause: Per-touchMove integer-pixel scroll quantization in the fork (std::lround of delta-since-last-move), so slow/small/jittery moves round to zero and big moves lurch
contributors.evidence: Directly explains 'erratic / up-and-down / slow even on big movements' which is NEITHER fps nor RTT. WebPage.cpp:4278-4280 computes the scroll delta per touchMove as sdx = std::lround(m_driftstackLastTouchPoint.x - pos.x) (delta SINCE the last move, integer-rounded) and only scrolls if (sdx || sdy). Consequences: (1) scroll is driven by inter-move deltas, so while the box drains a BACKLOG the deltas are tiny and lround-to-zero -> no scroll, then a catch-up move -> a lurch = up-and-down jerk. (2) The fork has NO momentum (bus W2736: 'scrollBy(per-move delta), no fork momentum'), so a big finger sweep only scrolls by the net pixels actually delivered as discrete moves; dropped moves (touchMove is reliable=false, livekit-input-capture.ts:467) or rounded-away deltas mean a large sweep scrolls little ('big scroll only scrolls a little', bus W2747). (3) tapSlop=18px (WebPage.cpp:4252) swallows the first 18px of every drag as potential-tap before scroll commits = a start-of-scroll dead-band. (4) reliable=false moves never retransmit -> scroll silently under-shoots the finger. Magnitude: at ~12 delivered moves/s with sub-pixel deltas lrounding to 0, a moderate-speed drag can net near-zero scroll until it speeds up = erratic.

contributors.cause: Trans-Atlantic RTT (~150ms) on BOTH the input leg (mouse->box) and the video-return leg, so the felt finger-to-pixel loop carries ~150ms pure network round-trip
contributors.evidence: US box + EU user = ~150ms RTT (A3 verdict wpiyo8v6x; memory project_streaming_taps_a3_verdict). The felt scroll loop crosses the Atlantic TWICE: the touchMove travels ~75ms one-way over the LiveKit DataChannel to the box, and the resulting scrolled frame ~75ms back over the media path. So even with instant box processing and infinite fps, finger-to-pixel feedback carries the full ~150ms RTT. This is the founder's 'awful latency, much scrolling after I'm done' (bus W2741). A2/A3 agree the EU box is the #1 latency lever (bus W2741/W2744) but it is founder-gated infra. ~150ms is at the upper edge of feels-laggy for direct manipulation (humans notice >100ms on drag-to-track). MAJOR not dominant because, as the founder intuited (latency is not the only problem), at 12fps + per-move serialization it would still feel choppy/erratic even co-located.

contributors.cause: SCStream change-driven capture can STARVE frames exactly during a scroll, and bufferingNewest(8) drops oldest under encode/transport backpressure
contributors.evidence: CaptureLoop filters to status==.complete and drops .idle/.blank (CaptureLoop.swift:512,764), correct for idle pages but it means capture rate IS repaint rate; if the fork coalesces repaints during a fast scroll, capture delivers fewer distinct frames exactly when motion happens. The ordered hand-off uses .bufferingNewest(8) (CaptureLoop.swift:275) dropping the OLDEST un-consumed frame under encode/LiveKit backpressure (favors freshness, right for latency) so a CPU spike during scroll (software VP8 + per-move WD POSTs competing for CPU) can silently drop scroll frames. The box was also CPU-starved by macOS Spotlight indexing (load 20->2 after mdutil -i off; memory project_box_spotlight_cpu_starvation + bus W2737), a confound that skewed earlier measurements. Minor vs the 12fps supply + per-move serialization (second-order amplifier, and bufferingNewest is the correct latency tradeoff). Loss/jitter are healthy (0.1% loss, 15ms jitter, direct UDP per bus W2742), so the jitter buffer itself is not the problem.

contributors.cause: GUI-side input shaping: deadzone/commit gate and disabled-then-retuned momentum fling added felt lag and over/under-scroll on click-drag (largely resolved)
contributors.evidence: The GUI click-drag path historically added start-of-scroll latency: the commit gate required held>DRAG_HOLD_MS (was 140ms) before emitting any touchMove (livekit-input-capture.ts:170,438-441), so a scroll did not begin until ~140ms after the finger moved; A2 cut it to ~35ms in the W2747 overhaul. The inertial fling (computeFlingPath, livekit-input-capture.ts:217) was DISABLED (FLING_ENABLED=false, line 196) after it over-drove the fork per-move scroll -> 'much scrolling after I am done' (bus W2741), then re-enabled tightly-gated (W2747). The wheel path previously emitted one swipe per wheel event and the fork added swipeMomentumPath to every swipe -> ~100 stacked momentum swipes/s -> 'randomly scrolls back up' (bus W2736/W2740, now one continuous touchStream). Per A2 W2747 the input path is now 'no longer a factor', so MINOR/largely-resolved, but it was a real historical contributor and a regression here re-introduces erratic scroll. The from-START deadzone correctly matches the fork slop-from-start.

options.name: rAF-coalesce touchMove emit + multi-tick /actions batch
options.dealbreaker: The proposal's core premise — that smoothness is gated by an input "POST storm / head-of-line backlog" so the finger lags the cursor — is contradicted by the codebase owner's own deep analysis posted TODAY (A2 W2748, 2026-06-22, in /Users/john/code/driftstack/operations/agent-bus/A2-A3-BUS.md). With a live healthy pipeline (decode 30fps, latency 20ms, jitter 11ms, 0 freezes, udp·direct) manual scrolling is STILL "not smooth at all," and A2 states verbatim: "At 30fps the box renders the cumulative scroll position each frame, so GUI move-cadence/coalescing can't fix it (I checked — it's placebo)." The proposed rAF-coalesce + multi-tick batch IS that already-tested-and-rejected placebo. The real jank lives in the fork: WebPage.cpp:4275-4314 turns EVERY injected TouchMove into an immediate naive view->scrollBy(delta) / scrollToPositionWithoutAnimation(delta) — no compositor animation, no momentum, no per-frame integration — and that cumulative position is what gets repainted each frame. How the deltas arrive on the wire (one-per-event vs N-coalesced-per-POST) does not change the per-frame-sampled scroll position the user sees, so it cannot fix the choppiness the founder actually reports.
options.reasoning:
VERIFIED MECHANISM (not memory): (1) GUI emit path — apps/gui-client/src/lib/livekit-input-capture.ts onMouseMove (L418-468) sends one touchMove per DOM mousemove over the LiveKit DataChannel via sendInputEvent (livekit.ts L94, publishData reliable:false). (2) Box receive path — DataChannelInputReceiver is an actor; LiveKitVideoPublisher (L101-109, 377-381, 840-856) funnels inbound through a SINGLE FIFO consumer (W1822) that awaits each receive() to completion. receive()→dispatch()→inj.touchStreamMove()→WebDriverClient.injectTouchStreamMove → synchronous POST /session/:id/actions with touchStreamMoveActions(duration: max(1,16)) (WebDriverClient.swift L681-704). So moves ARE serialized and each POST animate-blocks ~16ms — a real latency source. (3) Fork scroll — WebPage.cpp:4260-4319: per TouchMove, once past tapSlop(18) from the START point, it does view->scrollBy(IntSize(sdx,sdy)) or area->scrollToPositionWithoutAnimation(...) using this-move's delta. That is the jank: a naive per-event position write, no native scrolling-tree/momentum.

WHY THE OPTION FAILS:
- Wrong layer / placebo: smoothness is the fork's per-frame scrollBy rendered at the repaint clock. Coalescing the wire traffic leaves the SAME sequence of scrollBy deltas applied; the rendered cumulative position per frame is unchanged. A2 already empirically checked this ("placebo").
- Founder/A2 already moved past latency: founder says "I don't think latency is the only problem," and the live readout (20ms RTT, 30fps, 0 freezes) shows the link is healthy yet it's still janky. So even the genuine latency win this option offers does not touch the reported symptom.
- It can make scrolling COARSER: collapsing N raw points to fewer larger deltas (with duration:0/1 ticks) feeds the fork bigger per-step scrollBy jumps (delta computed from m_driftstackLastTouchPoint, WebPage.cpp:4278) — fewer, chunkier position writes = potentially MORE stair-stepping, the opposite of smooth.
- No tap/scroll benefit: the fork commits tap→scroll on the FIRST move >tapSlop FROM START (WebPage.cpp:4263); batching doesn't change that classification, and the GUI already buffers taps cleanly (deadzone-from-start, ff90d18c).

WHAT'S ACCURATE IN THE PROPOSAL: fingerprintSafe:true is correct — this is operator-input timing, never a target-site-visible surface (touch coherence is preserved as long as start-before-moves/end-after ordering holds, which the W1822 FIFO already guarantees). engCost:low is also fair. But low-cost work on an already-disproven lever is misdirection that risks crowding out the actual fix.

THE ACTUAL FIX (per A2 W2748 asks to A1/A3): route injected touches into the fork's NATIVE scroll machinery (the scrolling tree / EventHandler pan path a real touch hits) so scrolling gets compositor-driven smoothing + momentum, instead of WebProcess-level scrollBy-per-move. Secondary hygiene worth doing independently of this proposal: drop the touchStreamMove duration 16→0/1 to stop the per-POST animate-block, and confirm SCStream repaint cadence holds DURING an active scroll. Those address latency, not the headline jank.

NOTE on a stale claim inside the proposal's own risk text ("the finger position the fork sees stops lagging the cursor"): that describes a latency symptom, but the founder's reproduction is jank at low latency — so the proposal is solving a problem the founder is not currently blocked on.

options.name: Send a high-level scroll command (scrollBy N) instead of per-touchMove, with box-side smoothing
options.dealbreaker: The box-side "momentum/easing" half of this option was already built, enabled, then DELIBERATELY DISABLED for the exact failure mode the option re-proposes — and the option targets the input wire, not the stated root cause (12fps SUPPLY-limited video). In /Users/john/code/driftstack-api/apps/gui-client/src/lib/livekit-input-capture.ts: FLING_ENABLED=false (line 196) with the comment "the founder hit 'awful latency, much scrolling AFTER i'm done' — the glide over-drove the fork's per-move scroll (A3 W2736)." The fork ALSO already applies its own momentum to every `swipe` (BehavioralRhythm.swipeMomentumPath), which is precisely why the wheel path was moved OFF `swipe` onto a continuous touchStream. So "the box can accumulate sub-pixel deltas and apply momentum/easing locally" is a re-tread of a tried-and-reverted approach; any easing/momentum re-introduces the over-scroll-after-release the founder already rejected. Meanwhile the founder's own diagnosis ("latency is not the only problem", fps is supply-limited by fork repaint + software VP8) is a DOWNSTREAM video-feedback problem this input-side change cannot touch — smoother input into a 12fps mirror still reads as choppy.
options.reasoning:
I verified the option's claims against the actual code, and the picture is more nuanced than the option presents.

WHAT THE OPTION GETS RIGHT (verified):
- The std::lround quantization bug is real, at the exact cited location (/Users/john/code/webkit-driftstack/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebPage/WebPage.cpp:4278-4280): per-move integer deltas mean a slow drag of <0.5px/move nets zero scroll. Accumulating float deltas would genuinely fix slow-drag dead-zones.
- The per-move serialization cost is real and worse than the option states: each touchMove is its OWN HTTP POST to the WebDriver /actions endpoint on the box (WebDriverClient.injectTouchStreamMove -> postJSON "/session/<id>/actions"). That is the dominant per-move cost, not DataChannel framing. Collapsing N moves/frame into one delta command genuinely removes N-1 round-trips-to-localhost-WD per frame. Legitimate efficiency win.
- The fingerprint-safety argument is sound IF the constraint in `risk` is honored: it MUST still drive the existing touch->native-scroll path (view->scrollBy), never a JS executeScript scrollBy (forbidden, W1453). The target site sees the same trusted native scroll regardless of wire format. Fingerprint risk is genuinely low.

WHAT THE OPTION OMITS / GETS WRONG (the load-bearing problems):
1. ALREADY LARGELY BUILT. The GUI wheel/trackpad path (onWheel, livekit-input-capture.ts:546-574) ALREADY accumulates wheel deltas into ONE continuous virtual-finger touch drag, with per-event delta clamping (+/-120) and edge re-centering for long scrolls. For the trackpad/wheel case (the dominant "scrolling feels bad" complaint) the "send an accumulated delta" idea is substantially implemented. The remaining delta is the float-accumulation in the fork (the lround fix) plus possibly collapsing the click-drag path.

2. THE SMOOTHING HALF WAS TRIED AND REVERTED. "Box can apply momentum/easing locally" directly re-proposes FLING_ENABLED (computeFlingPath + cancellable runtime), which exists but is set false because it over-drove the fork's per-move scroll and caused post-release drift the founder explicitly rejected ("much scrolling after i'm done"). The fork's per-swipe momentum (swipeMomentumPath) caused the same jumpy/overshoot, which is documented as why the wheel path abandoned `swipe`. Any "eased step" or local momentum re-opens this. The safe version is ONLY the 1:1 proportional delta (no easing/momentum) - i.e. strip the most-touted part of the smoothness payoff.

3. DOESN'T ADDRESS THE STATED ROOT CAUSE. Context says fps is SUPPLY-limited (WebContent repaint cadence, change-driven SCStream, possibly software VP8) and the founder says latency isn't the only problem. This option is purely input-side. Even a perfect scroll-intent command renders into a 12fps video mirror; the user still sees choppy feedback. "smoothnessPayoff: large" is overstated - the real payoff is "fixes slow-drag dead-zone + cuts per-move WD POSTs," not "makes manual mode smooth." A3's hardware-H.264 + repaint-cadence work is what actually attacks the stated bottleneck; this is complementary cleanup, not the fix.

NET: A worthwhile, low-risk efficiency/correctness improvement (the lround float-accumulation fix especially), but mis-scoped as a smoothness solution. Do the 1:1 proportional-delta + sub-pixel accumulation; do NOT re-add box-side momentum/easing (proven regression). Pair it with the supply-side (fps) work, which is the actual prerequisite for "very smooth."

Relevant files: /Users/john/code/webkit-driftstack/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebPage/WebPage.cpp (lines 4260-4319, touch->native-scroll + lround quantization); /Users/john/code/driftstack-api/apps/gui-client/src/lib/livekit-input-capture.ts (onWheel accumulation already built; FLING_ENABLED=false reverted momentum); /Users/john/code/driftstack/harness/Sources/BrowserController/WebDriverClient.swift (injectTouchStreamMove = one /actions POST per move); /Users/john/code/driftstack/harness/Sources/BrowserController/ManualTouchInjector.swift (streamMode incremental vs buffered); /Users/john/code/driftstack-api/packages/api-types/src/agent-input-event.ts (InputEvent union already has wheel + swipe; a new scroll {dx,dy} would be additive and cross-surface/SDK/Swift-decoder parity-bound).

options.name: Pipeline the box inbound consumer for input (coalesce-drop-stale touchMoves off the FIFO)
options.dealbreaker: It targets the wrong bottleneck for the founder's actual complaint. The per-touchMove WD POST goes to 127.0.0.1 (WebDriverClient host defaults to "127.0.0.1", request() builds http://127.0.0.1:port) — the fork's WebDriver server runs ON THE SAME BOX as the fork. So the inbound input round-trip is NOT subject to the ~150ms EU<->US RTT at all; it's a local-loopback POST (sub-ms to low-ms) plus the W3C pointerMove "duration" the body carries (default 16ms in touchStreamMoveActions). The founder's stated symptoms — "~12 fps reaching the GUI," "still not good," "latency isn't the only problem" — are about the OUTBOUND video supply cadence (SCStream change-driven repaint + software VP8), which this option does not touch. Input injection on a healthy box is already cheap and local; serializing a handful of local POSTs is not what makes scrolling feel choppy. This is a robustness/edge-case fix (a WD STALL won't wedge the whole input queue) mis-marketed as a "large smoothness payoff." On the normal path it buys little; the perceived lag is dominated by the video frames the user sees, not by input latency the user can't see.
options.reasoning:
I verified every load-bearing claim against the actual source (harness/Sources/StreamingBridge/LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift, DataChannelInputReceiver.swift, BrowserController/ManualTouchInjector.swift, WebDriverClient.swift).

WHAT'S ACCURATE in the proposal:
- The serial FIFO is real. LiveKitVideoPublisher.swift:377-383 drains one AsyncStream serially, awaiting each dispatchInboundData→ir.receive→dispatch→inj.touchStreamMove→client.injectTouchStreamMove→blocking postJSON. A WD stall on one move does block the next read. The W1822 comment block (lines 101-108) confirms the FIFO was added precisely to stop touch reordering (the per-message Task{} spawn race where a move could land before its start).
- The proposal's safety framing is the correct one: keep touchStart/touchEnd strictly ordered+reliable, only coalesce/drop the lossy moves between them. That IS the right design and it does respect the exact W1822 hazard. Fingerprint-safe is true: this is harness-side queue scheduling, zero JS/render change, no surface touched. engCost medium is fair.

WHY IT'S ONLY MARGINAL, not a smoothness win:

1. WRONG BOTTLENECK (the dealbreaker). Input POSTs are to 127.0.0.1 (WebDriverClient.swift:1010 + host default "127.0.0.1"). No trans-Atlantic RTT on the input leg. The 12fps/choppy complaint is the outbound video supply path (SCStream cadence + VP8), which A3 is already chasing with HW H.264. This option cannot move the fps the user sees. Coalescing local sub-ms POSTs yields a payoff far smaller than "large."

2. CROSS-POST POINTER PERSISTENCE IS UNVERIFIED — and coalescing makes it WORSE. WebDriverClient.swift:668-670 explicitly flags that incremental streaming "relies on the fork's WebDriver persisting pointer-DOWN state across /actions POSTs — VERIFY at drive-bridge bring-up; fallback = buffered mode." The whole incremental path (the one this option optimizes) is on shaky verified ground. If the fork does NOT persist DOWN state across POSTs, the system is forced into .buffered StreamMode (ManualTouchInjector.swift:57-67), where ALL moves are accumulated and emitted as ONE injectTouchPath on touchEnd. In buffered mode, dropping intermediate moves directly degrades the rendered drag path — coalescing is actively harmful there, not neutral. The option's payoff is contingent on an unverified property that may not even hold.

3. DROPPING MOVES CHANGES THE GESTURE SHAPE = a behavioral-coherence risk. The fork scrolls natively per-touchMove delta (W1453, ManualTouchInjector.swift:148-151 — no JS scrollBy; native touch->scroll). Coalesce-to-freshest collapses the velocity profile: native momentum/fling and scroll inertia are computed from inter-touchMove timing+distance. Cloud-gaming "latest-wins" works for an absolute cursor position; a touch DRAG is a path whose velocity is semantically meaningful (fling distance, rubber-banding). Dropping the intermediate samples can make a slow drag read as a teleport-then-stop, killing native inertia and producing a NON-HUMAN motion path — the exact jerky-path tell W1822's comment (lines 104-105) warns is "launch-critical." # Manual-mode smoothness: decisive architecture answer

## (1) Honest root cause — it is NOT mostly latency+fps anymore

The root-cause breakdown you were handed (12fps supply-limited, RTT-dominant) describes the system as of ~24h ago. **It is now stale.** Today's founder live readout (bus W2748, 2026-06-22):

```
23 fps · latency 20 ms · decode 30 fps · loss 0.4% · jitter 11ms · freezes 0 · transport udp · direct
```

The stream is **healthy**: 30fps decode, 20ms RTT, zero freezes, direct UDP. H.264 already landed. The frame-pump already shipped. And scrolling is *still* "not smooth at all." So:

- **fps is largely SOLVED** (30fps decode, not 12). The remaining repaint-during-scroll question is a second-order tail, not the headline.
- **RTT is NOT the bottleneck** — proven twice: 20ms live RTT this run, and the founder's own NL→US RDP-over-the-same-path "1000x faster" experiment. RDP hides RTT with local echo + its own frame clock; we lack neither badly enough to explain jank at 20ms.
- **The real structural defect is in the fork's touch→scroll handler**, verified in code at `/Users/john/code/webkit-driftstack/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebPage/WebPage.cpp:4260-4319`:
  - Every injected touchMove does a **synchronous main-thread `view->scrollBy(IntSize(sdx,sdy))`** (line 4313) or `scrollToPositionWithoutAnimation` (4311) — a raw position write, NOT WebKit's native compositor/scrolling-tree scroll. iOS smoothness comes from threaded compositor scrolling + UIScrollView momentum; this path has neither.
  - `TouchEnd: break;` (4321) — **zero momentum/inertia**. A flick stops dead.
  - `std::lround` per-move integer delta + `if (sdx || sdy)` gate (4278-4280) — **sub-pixel/slow moves round to zero and are dropped**, then a catch-up move lurches = the "erratic/up-and-down" the founder reports.

**The structural issue: the box renders the cumulative scroll position once per frame from a per-event `scrollBy`. That is intrinsically stair-stepped and momentum-less, and no amount of input coalescing, codec choice, or RTT reduction changes it.** A2 already empirically confirmed input coalescing is placebo here (W2748).

## (2) SHIP-NOW path — highest smoothness-per-effort, fingerprint-safe

Two changes, both in the fork (`webkit-driftstack`, owner A1, A3 coordinating), both inside the existing W1453 native-scroll path so the moat is untouched (target site still sees only genuine trusted engine scroll, no JS, no wheel):

**A. Sub-pixel delta accumulation (cheap, do first).** Replace the `std::lround`-per-move + `if (sdx||sdy)` drop with a carried fractional remainder (`m_driftstackScrollRemainderX/Y` as doubles): accumulate `lastTouch - pos` in float, apply the integer part, carry the fraction. Kills the round-to-zero dead-zone and the lurch. ~20 lines, low risk, directly attacks the "erratic even on big movements" symptom. This is necessary but not sufficient.

**B. Route injected touches through the native scrolling machinery (the real fix).** Stop calling raw `scrollBy`/`scrollToPositionWithoutAnimation`. Instead drive the target `ScrollableArea` through its `ScrollAnimator` (`scrollAnimator().scroll(...)` / the smooth-scroll path that the compositor/scrolling tree uses), and on `TouchEnd` (currently a bare `break;` at line 4321) hand the accumulated velocity to the platform momentum/`ScrollAnimator` kinetic path so a flick glides and decelerates like iOS. `m_useAsyncScrolling`/`ScrollingCoordinator` already exist in this fork (WebPage.cpp:1033, 7144); the injected-touch path is the one place bypassing them. This is the change that makes scrolling *feel* like an iPhone.

**Fingerprint safety:** both stay engine-side trusted scroll (no JS `executeScript`, the W1453 hard rule). Momentum MUST reuse the existing capture-grounded flick curve already pinned on the agent path (`operations/touch-capture/FINDINGS.md` §3 / W1902: peakBase ~20px, adaptive decay) — do NOT invent a second momentum model (a divergent constant-velocity/0ms fling is a behavioral tell, and a second model is exactly the W431/W433 divergence risk). This makes B behavioral-data-gated, but the data already exists.

**Owner split:** A1 owns the scrolling-engine wiring (B); A3 has been doing the injector/`WebPage.cpp` touch work and should pair. A2's GUI input is already clean (W2747/W2748) — nothing more needed there for the core fix.

## (3) Bigger architectural bets, in order

1. **Native scroll routing + momentum (B above)** — the actual fix. Do now.
2. **EU / per-region box** — founder-gated infra. NOT the smoothness fix (20ms RTT proves it), but it IS required for global customers (Asia/Oceania at 250-300ms cannot be served smoothly by any of this). Roadmap, not blocker.
3. **Client-side scroll prediction / local frame-shift (CSS-transform the `<video>`, reconcile on real frame)** — defer until AFTER 1 lands and is measured. It only hides open-loop RTT, which today is 20ms and not the complaint; it has no ground-truth scroll-offset to reconcile against (PageState carries no scroll position), so it rubber-bands on boundaries/sticky-headers/nested scrollers. Reconsider only if a residual remains after native scroll + an EU box, and only paired with a box-streamed scroll-offset signal.
4. **Zero-copy capture + repaint-cadence-during-scroll keepalive** — fleet-density CPU/headroom wins, do for scaling, not for single-session feel.
